narrative: Star Vetter automatically identifies candidate eclipsing binary stars in data from NASA's TESS satellite. An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars orbiting each other, where their orbital plane aligns with Earth so that one star regularly passes in front of the other, dimming the light we receive. TESS observes hundreds of thousands of stars, and this project works through that data systematically, applying statistical tests to separate real eclipsing binaries from noise and artifacts. Each candidate passes through multiple stages: statistical vetting to confirm the signal is real, cross-checking against six known variable-star catalogs to avoid re-announcing known objects, and an automated pixel-level check to rule out contamination from nearby stars. So far, the pipeline has confirmed 217 candidates from a sample of over 15,000 targets, representing 1.7% of TESS's full target list. While this process is rigorous, individual candidates may carry caveats; check each candidate's page for details.

faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary star?
faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a system of two stars orbiting each other. Their orbital plane is tilted so that from Earth's viewpoint, one star regularly passes in front of the other, blocking some of its light. This creates a predictable dip in brightness at regular intervals. By studying these dips - their depth, duration, and timing - astronomers can learn about the stars' sizes, orbital period, and how they interact.

faqs.question: What does 'candidate' mean here, and how is it different from 'confirmed'?
faqs.answer: A 'candidate' is a potential eclipsing binary that meets initial statistical criteria in the light curve data. A candidate is 'confirmed' when it survives an automated pixel-level check - a test that rules out false signals caused by nearby stars contaminating the measurement. Being confirmed on this site means the signal is real and on-target, but does not imply scientific verification by other means or follow-up.

faqs.question: What is the machine learning score I see on candidate pages?
faqs.answer: Star Vetter includes a machine learning model trained on 2,224 labeled examples that provides a second opinion on whether a candidate is likely real. It outperforms the baseline statistical rules used in the main pipeline. However, this score is informational only - it does not gate which candidates get checked, and it is not used to filter or prioritize results. All candidates that pass the statistical and contamination checks are listed regardless of their ML score.

faqs.question: How does Star Vetter check whether a candidate is real?
faqs.answer: After a candidate passes statistical vetting and is confirmed to be novel (not already in known catalogs), it undergoes an automated pixel-level check. This test examines the spatial distribution of the light signal across the detector to confirm the eclipse is coming from the target star itself and not contaminated by nearby stars. This entire process is automatic and requires no human intervention.

faqs.question: I notice a candidate has an unusual period - what does that mean?
faqs.answer: Sometimes the light curve could match two different orbital periods (an 'alias'). To check for this, Star Vetter compares the brightness dips from odd-numbered eclipses against even-numbered eclipses. If they differ significantly, the candidate may have a period alias - meaning the true orbital period could be half or twice what appears in the data. Such caveats are noted on individual candidate pages.

faqs.question: Can I verify a candidate myself?
faqs.answer: Yes. Star Vetter provides the TESS sector, camera, and CCD information for each confirmed candidate, as well as the orbital period and relative eclipse depths measured from the light curve. With this information and access to TESS data (freely available from MAST at NASA), you can download the raw light curve and inspect it yourself.

faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it appears on this site?
faqs.answer: Being listed on Star Vetter is the end of what this automated pipeline itself does. The site does not conduct or coordinate follow-up observations, submit results to scientific journals, or track whether other researchers study these objects. Confirmed candidates remain here as a catalog for anyone interested in eclipsing binaries found in TESS data.
